source.description: Bundled normative quality bar. Clause identifiers below name section and bullet; the complete requirement text is retained here.

clauses.quotation: OSI-approved license (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, or equivalent). Copyleft (GPL/AGPL) is not acceptable for components surfaced from VS.
Public source repository for the shipped versions.
All transitive dependencies must use OSI-approved, non-copyleft licenses. The SBOM (section 2) serves as the authoritative inventory.
NuGet packages must populate PackageLicenseExpression, RepositoryUrl, RepositoryCommit (commit SHA), Authors, and ProjectUrl.
Signed assemblies. All shipped assemblies are strong-name signed and Authenticode-signed using the partner's verified publisher identity.

Signed NuGet packages. All shipped .nupkg files are NuGet-signed for package integrity. For a working pattern using GitHub Actions and a free Azure Trusted Signing account, see .NET code & NuGet signing in GitHub Actions.

Publish without long-lived secrets. Use OIDC-based trusted publishing (e.g., NuGet.org Trusted Publishing) rather than storing API keys in CI. Reference walkthrough: Publishing NuGet packages from a GitHub Action without secrets.

SBOM with every release. Publish an SPDX or CycloneDX SBOM enumerating direct and transitive dependencies. For .NET libraries the easiest path is the Microsoft.Sbom.Targets MSBuild package, which is what .NET uses; see Generating SBOMs for .NET apps and NuGet packages.

Clean, attributable dependency graph. Every binary in the package is either (a) built from source in the partner's public repository, or (b) a referenced NuGet/npm package with a clear upstream. No unattributed binaries.

Documented threat model and security review. Maintain a security/threat model for the library and complete a security review before shipping. All identified threats and review findings must be addressed (or explicitly accepted with documented justification) before release.

Coordinated disclosure. Publish a SECURITY.md with a private disclosure contact, following the same coordinated-disclosure principles the .NET repos use: vulnerabilities are reported privately, fixed in private, and disclosed only after a fix is available.

Vulnerability response. Ship fixes for known vulnerabilities in line with the .NET security servicing cadence (typically the next monthly Patch Tuesday release after a fix is ready). Critical issues with known exploitation may warrant an out-of-band release.

Vulnerability scanning. Run dependency scanning on every release (e.g., dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive, GitHub Dependabot, or equivalent); running on every PR as well is optional but recommended. Do not ship with known unpatched High/Critical CVEs in any dependency, direct or transitive.
No surprise network calls. Components do not phone home, send telemetry, or load remote scripts/styles/fonts at runtime by default. Any telemetry must be opt-in and documented.

Render-mode-aware security. Component library authors must understand and follow Blazor's render-mode security model. Review and apply the relevant guidance from Threat mitigation guidance for static server-side rendering and Threat mitigation guidance for interactive server-side rendering.

Bundled third-party JS/CSS. It is common (and acceptable) to include compiled JS/CSS under wwwroot/ in a Razor Class Library. When that JS/CSS originates from a third-party library, the package must list the upstream component and version in the SBOM and preserve any license/notice files required by that component's license.

WCAG 2.2 Level AA conformance for all interactive components in their default configuration. This is the standard Microsoft applies to its own products and covers keyboard operability, semantic markup (ARIA roles, names, relationships), screen reader compatibility, color contrast, and use of color. No known AA failures at ship.
High contrast. Components remain usable in Windows High Contrast and CSS forced-colors mode.

Validation with Accessibility Insights. Run Accessibility Insights for Web against a representative sample app for each release. The FastPass must be clean, and at minimum one full Assessment is completed per major release.

Screen reader smoke test. Each major release is exercised with at least one screen reader (NVDA, JAWS, or Windows Narrator) to confirm announcements for state changes (selection, expansion, validation, async load).
Localization-ready. All user-visible strings are localizable. RTL layout support is optional but recommended.

Supported target frameworks. Must support the latest stable .NET release, ready on the day of GA. .NET previews are published well in advance so partners can be ready on release day. Supporting earlier .NET versions (in-support or out-of-support) is allowed and encouraged but not required; multi-targeting or separate package versions per .NET release are both fine.

Render mode coverage. Components work correctly under static SSR, Interactive Server, Interactive WebAssembly, and Auto, or clearly document the supported modes and fail with a clear compile-time or runtime error elsewhere. Prerendering must not throw.

Parameters. Use [Parameter] with { get; set; } auto-properties. Do not use required/init on parameters (BL0007). Do not mutate parameters from inside the component. Use [EditorRequired] where appropriate.
Events. Use EventCallback/EventCallback<T> (not Action/Func) for component events.

Lifecycle and async. Follow Blazor's async guidance: no .Result, .Wait(), Task.Run, ContinueWith, or Thread.Start on the renderer sync context. Use InvokeAsync + StateHasChanged for external events. Route errors from fire-and-forget work through ComponentBase.DispatchExceptionAsync.

Disposal. Components that own subscriptions, timers, CancellationTokenSource, or JS references must implement IAsyncDisposable and clean up. Catch JSDisconnectedException when disposing JS references.
JS interop. Use collocated .razor.js ES modules loaded from OnAfterRenderAsync. No JS interop in OnInitializedAsync. Dispose IJSObjectReference and DotNetObjectReference instances.
CSS isolation. Use .razor.css for component styles. Avoid inline style attributes. Do not pollute global CSS without a documented, prefixed surface.

Trimming and AOT. Component libraries must be prepared for trimming (set <IsTrimmable>true</IsTrimmable>, annotate reflection/dynamic code with the appropriate attributes) so apps using Interactive WebAssembly can trim and AOT-compile cleanly. See also the Blazor trimming guidance. Annotate or fix trim and AOT warnings rather than suppressing them.
Public API stability. Follow SemVer. Mark experimental APIs with [Experimental]. [Obsolete] APIs ship with guidance for at least one minor version before removal.

Diagnostics. The library itself builds clean — no new warnings on supported TFMs from the .NET analyzers or the Blazor BL* analyzers. (This is about the library's own code; consumer code calling [Obsolete] APIs intentionally is fine.)
Documentation. XML doc comments on all public APIs. Public docs site with samples for each component covering all supported render modes.

Minimize render work. Override ShouldRender where appropriate; avoid unnecessary StateHasChanged calls; keep render trees small. Don't trigger re-renders from every parameter change if the result is unchanged.
Use @key on lists and other repeated elements so the renderer can preserve element identity and avoid unnecessary teardown.
Avoid heavy work in OnParametersSet/render. Move expensive computation to async lifecycle methods or memoize results.
Virtualize large lists using <Virtualize> (or document how consumers can virtualize the component's content).
Be deliberate about cascading values. Cascading values re-render every consumer when they change — scope them narrowly or use IsFixed="true" when the value doesn't change.
Interactive Server cost awareness. Each Interactive Server circuit holds component state on the server. Keep per-component state small; avoid holding large object graphs in component fields.
WebAssembly download size. Keep the library's WASM-relevant surface trimmable (see section 4) and avoid pulling in large transitive dependencies that bloat published apps.

Partner scaffolders must integrate with dotnet scaffold — not dotnet new — and be contributed to the dotnet/scaffolding repo. They must meet the quality bar that repo applies to scaffolders shipped in the default set, including:
Generated code follows section 3 (accessibility) and section 4 (Blazor patterns).

Generated code may only take dependencies on the .NET platform and qualifying partner libraries (libraries that meet this quality bar). Generated code must not depend on other proprietary or closed-source libraries.
Generated projects reference signed packages from nuget.org (no preview-only, internal, or non-public feeds) and pin partner package versions.
No execution of arbitrary scripts during scaffolding.
Scaffolders are updated when the partner library is patched or otherwise updated in ways that affect the generated output.
Partner AI skills are contributed to the dotnet-blazor plugin in dotnet/skills and must meet that repo's contribution guidance (format, evals, ownership). In addition:
Responsible AI review. New skills must go through a Responsible AI (RAI) review before merge.
Release-day readiness. Skills are updated for each .NET release so they are accurate on release day.
Tracks the library. When the underlying partner library is patched or updated in ways that change recommended patterns, the corresponding skill is updated promptly.

No proprietary lock-in. Generated code may only take dependencies on the .NET platform and qualifying partner libraries (libraries that meet this quality bar). Generated code must not depend on other proprietary or closed-source libraries.

Active maintainer support. The library maintainer provides timely support for security, accessibility, and engineering issues, with a single published point of contact and a stated response SLA. Scaffolders and AI skills are updated promptly when the library is patched or otherwise updated.

End-of-life notice. Partners must publicly provide sufficient advance notice before ending support for the library so customers can plan migrations and Microsoft can remove the library from promotion.
Requirements verified each release. Requirements are re-checked at each release.

Issue transparency. Non-security accessibility bugs and other issues against shipped versions are tracked publicly (e.g., GitHub Issues with labels). Security issues follow the coordinated-disclosure process in section 2 and are not disclosed publicly until a fix is available.
Removal criteria. Microsoft may stop promoting a partner library if it no longer adheres to these requirements.
